capabilities.target: Chat reply to the authenticated requester
Jira tickets, including tickets filed by customers

inputs.source: Employee question via SSO-authenticated chat channel
Jira tickets filed by customers, via planned Jira MCP server

instructions.note: The only stated protection against leaking secrets or credentials is a prompt instruction; no structural secret-scanning or output filtering is described, and the instruction does not mention untrusted ticket content or egress destinations at all.

controls.name: No network egress exists today
controls.decay_rationale: No destination exists today for data to leave the organization's network, so this is not model-dependent; however it fails open the moment an egress-capable tool such as web.fetch is added, since the control is really 'no egress tool exists' rather than an enforced allowlist.

controls.name: Reply destination bound to the authenticated requester (SSO)
controls.decay_rationale: The chat reply's destination is the verified SSO identity of the requester, taken from the system of record, not from any model-controlled value, so a more capable or manipulated model cannot redirect the reply to another address.

controls.name: Chat client does not render images or fetch links
controls.decay_rationale: Removes a common covert exfiltration channel independent of model behavior; it only covers the current chat client and does not extend to a future web.fetch tool.

controls.name: Read-only credential for docs.search
controls.decay_rationale: The credential cannot write or delete regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Only engineers can write to design docs
controls.decay_rationale: Limits who can inject content into the confidential doc store, which is why in.design_docs is classified internal rather than untrusted; unaffected by model capability.

controls.name: Prompt instruction: never paste secrets or credentials
controls.decay_rationale: Relies entirely on model compliance; a more capable or adversarially prompted model can rationalize exceptions, and the instruction does not address ticket content or fetch destinations.

controls.name: Destination allowlist for web.fetch (not yet designed)
controls.decay_rationale: If implemented as a fixed allowlist not writable by the model or an attacker, this would sever the planned exfiltration path; nothing in the roadmap description indicates it is planned.

controls.name: Spotlighting/isolation of untrusted Jira ticket content (not yet designed)
controls.decay_rationale: Would reduce but not eliminate the chance that injected ticket text is treated as an instruction; still model-dependent even if added.

controls.name: Human approval gate on web.fetch when confidential data is in context (not yet designed)
controls.decay_rationale: A raw-action gate showing the literal destination and payload would not decay with model capability; nothing in the roadmap description indicates it is planned.

controls.name: Action logging for docs_search, chat_reply, and web.fetch (not yet designed)
controls.decay_rationale: Detective only; does not prevent anything but makes the future egress path observable.

findings.title: Confidential design-doc content reaches the chat reply, but the destination is bound to the authenticated requester and no egress exists today (T to S3, severed)

attack_path.note: Agent reads confidential design docs to answer
Agent replies with content derived from the confidential docs, delivered only to the same authenticated requester

forecast.watch_signal: Any configuration change that removes the no-egress restriction or changes chat delivery to a non-bound destination (for example enabling forwarding or broadening the recipient list), independent of the web.fetch/Jira additions tracked in the companion forecast finding.

evidence.observation: The design docs are confidential; only engineers can write to them, which is why in.design_docs is classified internal rather than untrusted.
Replies go only to the authenticated requester, and the chat client does not render images or fetch links, which binds the egress destination and removes covert exfiltration channels.
There is no network egress today and the credential is read-only, which severs the only S3-class path (confidential read combined with egress) that currently exists.

recommendations.action: Preserve the no-network-egress and destination-binding invariants as hard architectural constraints (network policy, not just application config) so they cannot be silently disabled.
Add action logging for docs_search and chat_reply so any future change in destination binding is independently observable.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1) opens if web.fetch and the Jira MCP server are added: customer-authored ticket text could direct exfiltration of confidential design docs

attack_path.note: A customer-filed Jira ticket contains attacker-crafted text (indirect prompt injection), ingested via the planned Jira MCP server
Agent retrieves the ticket content as context
Agent reads confidential design docs to answer the question, now alongside the injected instructions
Planned web.fetch tool constructs an outbound request, ostensibly for a 'public reference', that can encode confidential doc content to an attacker-controlled destination

forecast.watch_signal: Tool manifest diff showing a web.fetch entry, and/or MCP client config diff showing a new Jira server entry in the tools/list response.

evidence.observation: Roadmap: add a web.fetch tool so answers can include public references. This is a new, undescribed egress channel with no stated destination allowlist, approval gate, or sandboxing.
Roadmap: connect a Jira MCP server that includes tickets filed by customers. Customer-authored content is untrusted and would be ingested into the agent's context alongside internal tickets.

Current instructions only address not pasting secrets into answers; they say nothing about treating ticket content as untrusted or about validating web.fetch destinations, so the existing behavioral control does not cover this new path.

recommendations.action: Before shipping web.fetch, restrict destinations to a fixed allowlist of vetted public documentation domains; never let the model construct an open URL from retrieved content.

Add a raw_action human approval gate on web.fetch calls made in any session where confidential design-doc content has been read, with the approver shown the literal destination URL and payload, not a model summary.
Isolate and label all Jira ticket content, especially customer-filed tickets, as untrusted data, and instruct the model never to treat ticket text as instructions.
Log every web.fetch destination and alert when a fetch follows a confidential-doc read in the same session.
Scope the Jira MCP credential to least-privilege read access, and keep customer-filed tickets in a clearly separated, labeled untrusted namespace distinct from internal engineering tickets.

rating.rationale: The present-day design is well-contained: the only path to an S3-class sink (confidential read combined with egress) is a benign reply delivered to the same already-authenticated requester, and today there is no network egress at all, so residual risk is low. Autonomy limits (step and runtime bounds) are not declared, so the inherent tier for that path is raised one step to high per the rubric's autonomy modifier. Two declared roadmap items change this picture: a web.fetch tool (a new, apparently unconstrained egress channel) and a Jira MCP server that ingests customer-filed, untrusted ticket content. Nothing in the roadmap description mentions a destination allowlist, an approval gate, or untrusted-content isolation accompanying either addition. If both are added as described, the no-network-egress control that currently makes the design safe no longer exists, and a classic lethal-trifecta path (untrusted ticket content, confidential doc read, open egress) becomes available at critical severity from day one of the change. This is a forecast-only finding: no such path exists in the artifacts reviewed today.

limitations: This assessment reflects declared design and configuration in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior.

The web.fetch tool and Jira MCP server are roadmap items; their actual implementation (argument schemas, credential scope, destination constraints) is unknown, so the forecast finding uses plausible default assumptions per the toxic-combinations search procedure and carries medium confidence.
No MCP config or tool manifest was provided for docs.search, so its exact capability scope is inferred from the system prompt and runtime notes.
No access control list for who may ask questions was provided; this assessment assumes the SSO-authenticated requester is the intended internal audience as stated in the runtime notes.
